name: Traveller Scottish
world_status: a description exists but is not accessible

sources.citation: McKean, Thomas A. 2021. Multi-Layered Communication and Function in Scottish Traveller Cant. Traditiones 50(2): 93-120. doi:10.3986/traditio2021500206
sources.note: Nothing. Ethnological/functional account (Cant as Scots-embedded in-group lexis; 'interacts with the Scots language'); no phonology. Its reference list confirms Clement 1981 (GLS 15:17-25), Douglas 2002 (pp.125-138) and Kirk & Falconer 2002 (pp.132-137) in Kirk & O Baoill (eds.).

sources.citation: Lewis, M. Paul (ed.). 2009. Ethnologue: Languages of the World, 16th ed., entry 'Traveller Scottish' [trl] (Wayback capture 2012).
sources.note: Nothing; comments only 'Blend of High Romani and Elizabethan Cant. Earliest texts go back to 16th century.'

sources.citation: Matras, Yaron, Hazel Gardner, Charlotte Jones & Veronica Schulman. 2007. Angloromani: A different kind of language? Anthropological Linguistics 49(2): 142-184 (author PDF via Wayback of romani.humanities.manchester.ac.uk).
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: online with a university library login (also: harvard online access (harvardkey); publisher (doi, likely paywalled))
sources.note: About Angloromani (angl1239), not Scottish Cant: 'forward shift of stress' in Romani-derived words (kalo > 'kawla, balo > 'bawla) with final-vowel reduction. Mentions Scottish Travellers only as a separate group and cites Kirk & O Baoill 2002 for their Cant. Not usable for trav1235.

sources.citation: Matras, Yaron. 2004. Romani in the UK. BBC 'Languages of the UK' web text, 5 pp. (Wayback PDF).
sources.note: Nothing; notes Scottish Travellers do not use Romani proper.

sources.citation: Russell, Alexander. 1914-15. Scoto-Romani and Tinklers' Cant: Twenty sources arranged and edited. Journal of the Gypsy Lore Society, New Series 8: 11-79 (archive.org scanned of JGLS n.s. 8).
sources.note: Has a short 'Phonetics' section (p.13-14): compares the collectors' spelling systems, notes k/t interchange and liquid confusions, quotes Simson on vowel values; says nothing about word stress/accent. No accent remarks in the vocabulary (grep of the article range).

sources.citation: McCormick, Andrew. 1907. The Tinkler-Gypsies. Dumfries: J. Maxwell & Son (archive.org scanned, tinklergypsies00mcco).
sources.note: Tinkler-Gypsy (Galloway) Cant vocabulary prefaced only by a vowel-orthography key ('consonants... pronounced as in English'); nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Simson, Walter (ed. James Simson). 1865 [1878 printing]. A History of the Gipsies, with Specimens of the Gipsy Language. London: Sampson Low / New York (archive.org scanned, Cornell copy cu31924085204109).
sources.note: pp.315-16 only: 'The letter a is pronounced broad... like aw in paw...; and ie, or ee, in the last syllable of a great many words, are sounded short and quick; and ch soft, as in church.' No statement of stress placement.

sources.citation: Douglas, Sheila. 2002. Travellers' Cant in Scotland. In J. M. Kirk & D. P. O Baoill (eds.), Travellers and their Language, 125-138. Belfast: Clo Ollscoil na Banriona (with Kirk & Falconer, Scottish Cant Words, 132-137, same volume).
